entry.evidence: To understand the role of aerosols in the Archean climate we must under-stand which nucleation pathways were available.

sequences.source_document: Published paper (PDF body; XML text for abstract and captions)

steps.action: Asked which aerosol nucleation pathways were available in the low-oxygen Archean atmosphere, given that OH oxidation of SO2 needs O2.
steps.quote: To understand the role of aerosols in the Archean climate we must under-stand which nucleation pathways were available.

steps.action: Proposed SO2 photolysis by UV, then O + SO2 to SO3 and SO3 + H2O to H2SO4, as an O2-independent route to sulphuric acid (Reactions 2-4).
steps.quote: While oxidation of SO2 via OH may not have been viable, alternatives exist.

steps.action: Designed a 1 m3 chamber test: N2 with max 10 ppm O2, SO2 above modern levels (justified by Ueno et al. 2009), 253.7 nm UV lamps, humidifier, and PSM (~1.4 nm) plus CPC (~4 nm) detection.
steps.quote: Therefore we assume an SO2 concentration higher than today.

steps.action: Characterized chamber ionization with the G4beamline simulation code: about 3 ion pairs cm-3 s-1 background and about 42 with the 137Cs gamma sources exposed.
steps.quote: Using the G4beamline simulation code

steps.action: Set laboratory conditions: steady-state flows, UV bursts of 20 min (10 min in the ionization set) separated by long relaxation periods, one set varying SO2 and RH and one varying ionization at several UV levels.
steps.quote: Two main sets of experiments were performed.

steps.action: Estimated formation rates at each instrument cut-off from a linear fit to the rising side (20-80% of maximum) of each smoothed aerosol peak, following Tomicic et al. (2018).
steps.quote: The slope of the fit is then the formation rate.

steps.action: Repeated reference conditions (e.g. 80 ppb SO2) at the start, middle and end of series and used them to correct chamber drift with a linear term.
steps.quote: [...] same set of conditions were used to correct for drift caused by e.g. gradual changes in chamber impurities.

steps.action: Measured formation rates across 4 SO2 levels (40-105 ppb) and RH levels (0, 35, 51%); rates rose with both, and at 0% RH particles appeared only above 320 ppb SO2.
steps.quote: Formation rates increased with increasing levels of both SO2 and RH showing that both are needed for forming the nucleating molecules.

steps.action: Fitted ln(PSM formation rate) against ln[SO2] (slope 5.1, r2 0.99), giving a power-5 dependence, and inferred from the PSM/CPC ratio that SO2 and RH also aid growth.
steps.quote: This indicates that the formation rate depends on the [SO2] to the power of 5.

steps.action: Converted the SO2 scaling to an implied [H2SO4]^2.5 dependence, assuming H2SO4 scales as [SO2]^2, and compared it with published nucleation scalings.
steps.quote: which is closely in line with observations (Sipila et al., 2010; Kirkby et al., 2011)

steps.action: Checked for ozone production with a Teledyne T400 ozone analyzer at 100% UV; [O3] was no more than 0.1 ppb, judged insignificant.
steps.quote: Two separate measurements with a ozone analyzer (Teledyne T400) instead of the aerosol equipment were made with 20 min UV 100% power.

steps.action: Derived the expectation from chemistry that added O2 should lower H2SO4 production, because atomic O is consumed by forming O3.
steps.quote: The presence of oxygen should decrease the sulphuric acid production in our system as O can react with O2, producing O3.

steps.action: Raised [O2] to about 3800 ppm by adding air from two sources (filtered compressor air and bottled synthetic air).
steps.quote: The effect of oxygen was tested by adding 100 mL/min of air, mixed with 5.4 L/min of N2

steps.action: Compared the O2-test formation rates with the expectation: rates rose by up to a factor of 6, compressor air more than synthetic air, under large chamber drift.
steps.quote: In both cases the formation rates increased by a factor of up to 6, contrary to expectations.

steps.action: Kept the photolysis hypothesis and attributed the mismatch to an auxiliary: trace pollutants in the added air, in different amounts per source.
steps.quote: These results indicate that the oxygen-containing air contained trace pollutants assisting in the nucleation

steps.action: Varied ionization (gamma sources off or on) at four UV lamp settings, measured with the CPC only; the PSM was unavailable and UV intensity was not measured.
steps.quote: Similar series were made at 3 other UV settings and the results are shown in Table 2.

steps.action: Compared the results with the literature: rates rose with UV, as expected if photolysis drives nucleation, and the ionization effect was strongest at the lowest UV, consistent with published ion-induced nucleation.
steps.quote: the increase in formation rate due to increased ionization rate is consistent with ion-induced nucleation

steps.action: Modelled H2SO4 against SO2 with KINTECUS (113 reactions, sulphur and O-C-H chemistry after Ueno et al. 2009), with photolysis rates tuned to chamber UV and then reduced; 35% RH runs gave similar results.
steps.quote: 113 reactions were modelled including 7 photolysis reactions along with the sulphur chemistry and O–C–H chemistry described in Ueno et al. (2009).

steps.action: Compared the model's H2SO4-SO2 exponent (power law 1.8, r2 0.998) with the assumption behind the [H2SO4]^2.5 reading of the measured scaling.
steps.quote: thus supports the idea that formation rates at the PSM detection limit depends on

steps.action: Compared the RH dependence with Dunne et al. (2016): a factor of 10 from 35 to 51% RH against their factor of 2, while the model shows H2SO4 is insensitive to RH.
steps.quote: indicating a higher dependence on RH for this system

steps.action: Modelled the O2 effect: raising [O2] to 3800 ppm should significantly decrease H2SO4 and hence nucleation.
steps.quote: Modelling the effect of oxygen shows that increasing [O2] to 3800 ppm would decrease sulphuric acid significantly

steps.action: Used the model-measurement contrast to support the pollutant auxiliary, citing the earlier suspicion for this gas system (Tomicic et al. 2018).
steps.quote: This supports that the injected air contained unknown pollutants active in the formation (and growth) of the aerosols

steps.action: Estimated, from cited impurity levels and the Dunne et al. parametrization, that impurities raise measured rates by perhaps 1-2 orders of magnitude above a pure H2SO4-H2O system.
steps.quote: would lead to higher measured formation rates than expected for a pure sulphuric acid and water system by perhaps 1–2 orders of magnitude

steps.action: Kept the claim that sulphuric acid aerosol formation was possible in the Archean, given higher SO2 and UV, with UV and SO2 trading off.
steps.quote: This study shows that aerosol formation with the sulphuric acid system, which is prevalent today, was also possible back then

tree.answer: Whether sulphuric acid nucleation can occur without O2-dependent OH oxidation
No; the Archean atmosphere is unobservable, so a laboratory analogue is used
Test whether SO2 photolysis yields enough H2SO4 to nucleate at <10 ppm O2
No rival pathway stated; trace pollutants enter only as an auxiliary
Only the expectation that added O2 lowers rates, which was contradicted and attributed to pollutants
Conditions set in a laboratory chamber (SO2, RH, UV, ionization, O2)
Positive dependence holds across SO2, RH, UV and ionization; the O2 test is confounded by impurities and drift
Kept: nucleation possible, formation rate scaling as [SO2]^5

end.claim: Sulphuric acid nucleation by SO2 photolysis occurs at <10 ppm O2, with formation rates rising with SO2 (about [SO2]^5), RH, UV and ionization over the tested ranges, suggesting the pathway could have operated in the Archean.

decisive_move.sentence: Setting laboratory conditions of <10 ppm O2 with UV photolysis of elevated SO2 and controlled RH is what produced the observed nucleation bursts; without that set condition there is no claim.

gates.evidence: Action: the photolysis-pathway hypothesis (p. 2) directed the chamber design and the parameter variation (pp. 2-3). Claim: nucleation could have failed to appear at low O2, but the stated O2 expectation failed (p. 4) and was absorbed by an untested pollutant auxiliary, so the test of mechanism is partial. Registration: nothing is reported as fixed before the data.

imports.item: 137Cs gamma sources (25 MBq) to raise ionization
KINTECUS kinetics solver (v6.8) for a 113-reaction model
Mercury discharge UV lamps at 253.7 nm for SO2 photolysis

limits: The supplied XML text contains only the abstract and captions, so body steps are located by printed page. The paper uses no 'first' language. UV intensity was not measured, and the PSM was unavailable in the ionization set, so the ionization effect rests on CPC data alone; its ratios of 0.99-1.6 are mostly within about 2 standard deviations of 1. Particle losses (~15-50%) were not corrected. The O2 test was confounded by large drift, and the pollutant explanation is not tested directly (inference: it is an ad hoc auxiliary). Impurities may raise all rates by 1-2 orders of magnitude, which weakens the transfer to a pure Archean system. The extrapolation to the Archean is argued, not tested. Sub-claims and their statuses: [SO2]^5 scaling, regularity_in_range; [H2SO4]^~2.5 reading via the KINTECUS model, best_explanation; stronger RH dependence than Dunne et al., regularity_in_range; pollutants causing the O2 result, best_explanation without a test; ionization enhancement strongest at low UV, regularity_in_range with weak support. No review file or earlier version was supplied, so no review sequence is coded.

disagreements.target: Dunne et al. (2016) RH dependence of sulphuric acid nucleation (CLOUD parametrization)
disagreements.support: The PSM formation rate rose by a factor of 10 from 35 to 51% RH, against a factor of 2 in the Dunne parametrization, which the paper attributes to the high-SO2 chemistry of this system.
disagreements.quote: In this study the formation rate in the PSM (similar to the instrument used by Dunne et al. (2016)) increases by a factor of ten

alternatives_considered.chosen: No correction for sampling and chamber particle losses
alternatives_considered.alternatives: Correcting with loss estimates (~15% at 4 nm, ~50% at 1.4 nm, Tomicic et al. 2018)
alternatives_considered.reason: Losses apply equally to all measurements with an instrument, and the paper does not parametrize formation rates

alternatives_considered.chosen: Both air sources used for the O2 test
alternatives_considered.alternatives: External compressor air with charcoal and citric acid filtering vs bottled synthetic air

alternatives_considered.chosen: Photolysis rates fitted to UV fluxes from a similar chamber and then reduced
alternatives_considered.reason: To produce more realistic sulphuric acid concentrations

alternatives_considered.chosen: Both fits reported for modelled H2SO4 vs SO2
alternatives_considered.alternatives: 2nd-degree polynomial (r2 0.997) vs power law with exponent 1.8 (r2 0.998)
